newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan dismisses U.S. drug man release demand.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan dismisses U.S. drug man release demand.

text.p: Pakistan on Thursday rejected a U.S. demand for the release of a detained local employee of Washington's Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA) in what appears to be a developing diplomatic row between the two countries.

A Foreign Ministry spokesman called the demand for the release of Ayaz Baloch beyond the powers of the United States, while a newspaper seen as close to Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif warned Washington against treating Pakistan like Panama.

The row has erupted ahead of a planned visit to the United States next week by Pakistan Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan, whose engagements include meetings with Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, Defence Secretary William Cohen and National Security Adviser Samuel Berger.
The spokesman told a news briefing that Baloch, an employee of the DEA office at the U.S. embassy in Islamabad, was a Pakistani national and would be dealt with under Pakistani law.
"So the Americans, while they can express their views, cannot technically make such a request," he said when asked about the U.S. demand last weekend for the man's release.
"This is a matter which comes under the legal domain," the spokesman said at a regular briefing. "This is not a political issue."
Pakistani police arrested Baloch last week for alleged "involvement in drug trafficking and anti-state activities".

Islamabad has declined to explain the charges but has denied the arrest was in retaliation for the arrest of a senior Pakistan Air Force (PAF) officer in New York last month for allegedly carrying two kg (4.4 lb) of heroin in an air force plane.
Pakistan's English-language newspaper The Nation on Thursday accused the United States of overstepping the limits of legitimate activity, saying Pakistan was not Panama.
Washington invaded Panama in December 1989 to remove and arrest strongman General Manuel Noriega, now serving a 40-year jail term on drugs charges.

"The U.S. may have been able to get away with its flagrant violation of the independence and sovereignty of Panama in its bid to punish General Noriega for his alleged crimes of omission and commission, but it will do itself much good to remember that Pakistan is no Panama and neither is its elected leader a former protege-turned-rebel," a Nation editorial said.
A second air force officer was arrested in Pakistan after PAF chief Air Chief Marshal Abbas Khattak ordered a high-level inquiry into the incident.
